callouts.label: Plumbing
callouts.hint: Find the node on the far left where blue and gray pipes branch toward a sink, a toilet, and a floor drain.
callouts.description: Plumbing delivers water under pressure and carries waste out through sloped, vented drains (Chapter 14). It relies on the enclosure to keep pipes from freezing, on the structure to pass through framing, and on electricity for pumps and water heating. It also feeds fire protection, because sprinklers need an adequate water supply.

callouts.label: Occupants
callouts.hint: Find the node at upper left with a small group of adult figures beside a laptop, a coffee cup, and an open window.
callouts.description: People are the reason the building exists, and they change every system's load: breathing, heat from bodies and equipment, hot-water use, plug loads, and wear. Behavior such as opening windows, thermostat settings, or blocking exits can raise or erase the savings a design predicted. Thin dashed links run from this node to every other system.
callouts.tip: A design is only a prediction until real people move in.

callouts.label: Structure
callouts.hint: Find the top node, a small frame with a column, a beam, and a concrete footing.
callouts.description: Structure carries gravity, wind, and snow loads to the ground (Chapter 6) and supports the weight of the other systems: rooftop units, transformers, and rooftop solar panels. Pipes, ducts, and conduit must pass through it without weakening it, so each penetration of a beam or joist needs the structural engineer's approval (Chapter 16).
callouts.tip: Ask the structural engineer before you cut or drill a beam.

callouts.label: Structure to Fire Protection
callouts.hint: Find the medium-thick arrow between the top node and the upper-right node, with a small boxed wall section beside it.
callouts.description: The structural materials and the building's construction type set how much fire resistance each beam, column, and wall needs. Unprotected steel loses much of its strength in a developed fire, and heavy timber resists by charring. A sprinkler system can also earn an increase in allowable building area, so the two are chosen together (Chapter 18).

callouts.label: Fire Protection
callouts.hint: Find the node at upper right with a ceiling sprinkler head, a round smoke detector, and a thick rated wall section.
callouts.description: Fire protection combines passive containment (rated walls, floors, and doors) with active detection, alarm, sprinklers, and smoke control (Chapter 14). It depends on the others: structure and enclosure supply the rated assemblies, plumbing supplies the sprinkler water, electrical powers the alarm, and HVAC fans are shut down or switched to smoke control on an alarm.

callouts.label: Electrical
callouts.hint: Find the node on the far right with a gray switchboard, a row of breakers, and a utility meter.
callouts.description: Electrical brings power in at the service entrance and distributes it through panelboards to lights, fans, pumps, controls, and alarms (Chapters 15 and 16). Every added load, from a kitchen oven to a heat pump or an EV charger, has to fit within the service and be coordinated with the other design disciplines.
callouts.tip: The electrical designer is the last stop for every other trade's load.

callouts.label: Plumbing to Enclosure
callouts.hint: Find the medium-thick arrow on the lower left with a pipe crossing a wall section, a small snowflake, and a drip.
callouts.description: Pipes in exterior walls or unheated spaces can freeze in a cold snap, and a frozen pipe can burst. Keep water pipes on the warm side of the insulation (Chapter 11). Pipes also pierce the air control layer, so every penetration must be sealed, and a leak inside a wall wets an assembly that dries slowly.
callouts.tip: Keep supply pipes on the warm side of the insulation.

callouts.label: Enclosure
callouts.hint: Find the node at lower left with a wall section showing siding, a window, and a thick layer of insulation.
callouts.description: The enclosure (walls, roof, foundation, windows, and doors) separates inside from outside and controls rain, air, vapor, and heat (Chapters 11 and 12). Its quality sets how much heating and cooling the building needs, which makes it the first step in the efficiency order of Chapter 19. It also shelters every other system from weather.

callouts.label: Enclosure to HVAC
callouts.hint: Find the thickest arrow on the poster, curving along the bottom of the ring between the wall node and the red equipment node.
callouts.description: A better enclosure leaks less heat, so the heating and cooling loads shrink and smaller, right-sized equipment can do the job. A tight enclosure also leaks too little to ventilate itself, so it needs mechanical ventilation, ideally balanced with heat recovery (Chapters 14 and 19). Drawn thickest because it is the strongest link.
callouts.tip: Tighten the building first, then ventilate it on purpose.

callouts.label: Ripple Effect: Triple-Pane Windows
callouts.hint: Find the glowing violet chain along the bottom that runs from a window with three glass layers to a smaller red heating unit and a smaller gray panel, with a short gray arrow pushing back.
callouts.description: Triple-pane windows lose less heat, so the heating load falls, a smaller heating system can be chosen, and if it is electric it needs less of the electrical service. Pushing back: triple glazing costs more, its heavier units need sturdier frames, and it does not reduce ventilation load. Whether the net cost falls must be checked.
callouts.tip: Follow every change through every system before you count the savings.

callouts.label: HVAC
callouts.hint: Find the node at lower right with a rooftop unit, a branching duct, and a heat pump outdoor unit.
callouts.description: HVAC heats, cools, and ventilates to hold comfort and air quality (Chapter 14). Its size follows the loads set by the enclosure, the occupants, and the ventilation air, and its energy comes through the electrical system. It must also be coordinated with structure for weight and openings, and with fire protection for smoke control.

callouts.label: HVAC to Electrical
callouts.hint: Find the thick arrow on the right side with a small lightning-bolt shape, running from the red equipment node up toward the gray switchboard node.
callouts.description: Fans, pumps, compressors, and electric heat are among a building's largest electrical loads. The mechanical engineer gives the electrical designer an equipment schedule so wire and breakers can be sized (Chapter 16). Replacing fuel-fired heating with a heat pump moves heating onto the electrical service, which may then need more capacity.
callouts.tip: No wire or breaker is sized until the equipment schedule arrives.
